title: Anchored hotset sensitivity probe
body:
Context and quick summary:

This is a focused exploratory note on a specific phenomenon we've seen in production traces: a small subset of KV pages that are repeatedly accessed across long-running sessions and appear to be "anchored" in memory by repeated prefix reuse patterns. These pages are small in fraction of the total resident set (1-3%) but have outsized effect on bandwidth and eviction churn when their locality shifts.

Goal:
- Determine sensitivity of end-to-end latency and memory bandwidth to (a) anchoring heuristics (pin vs soft-pin), (b) time-to-evict thresholds for anchored pages, and (c) prefetch behavior when hotset center-of-mass shifts.
- Produce microbenchmarks and a short runbook of heuristics to test on dedicated pools.

Why this matters (practical):
- Observed incidents: during model rollouts with slightly different caching patterns, tail latency spikes correlated with sudden eviction of a handful of anchored pages.
- We suspect current LRU-ish eviction + global TTL causes oscillation when hotset migrates (small hotset move -> many pinned pages evicted -> re-warmburst -> bandwidth saturation).

Experiment plan (high level):
1) Synthesize workload traces that simulate anchored-access patterns and hotset shifts at different velocities (fast, medium, slow).
2) Run on local dev cluster and dedicated staging pool with instrumentation: per-page residency time, eviction count, KB/s per-channel, CPU stall due to paging, and request-level latency distribution.
3) Compare heuristics: baseline LRU, LRU+soft-anchor (deprioritize eviction for Xs after N hits), explicit pin (never evict unless memory pressure > Y), and decay-based unpin (exponential decay factor).
4) Measure costs: delta in throughput, extra memory used, extra query latency for cold misses, and bandwidth spikes during re-warm.

Microbenchmark details:
- Trace generator: small script that emits sequence of page accesses (page id namespace 0..500k). Hotset is 2k pages normally; anchor set 50 pages randomly sampled from hotset. Access pattern: Zipfian within hotset, Poisson arrival at client QPS 4000. Shift event: every T seconds shift anchor center by random offset drawn from Gaussian with sigma depending on velocity.
- Config knobs:
  * anchor-ttl (s): how long a page retains anchor score after last hit (0, 10, 60, 300)
  * anchor-strength: multiplier to keep page above eviction threshold (1.0 baseline, 2.0 soft-protect, inf=hard-pin)
  * eviction-watermark: percent of total mem used where aggressive eviction starts
  * prefetch-window: number of successive pages to prefetch when anchor moves

Instrumentation collected per run:
- per-request p50/p90/p99 latency (ms)
- per-page residency histogram (s)
- eviction rate (evictions/s)
- re-warm throughput (tokens/s) after shift
- device memory bandwidth (GB/s) over time
- CPU wait time on DMA/page-fill ops (ms total)
- number of page faults at OS/kernel level (for on-prem telemetry)

Preliminary runs (dev VM, QPS ~1k, quick):
- Baseline (LRU): frequent anchor shifts produced large eviction spikes; p99 increased by ~18-25% during shift windows. Eviction rate doubled for ~10s after shift, bandwidth spiked 1.7x.
- Soft-anchor (anchor-ttl=60s, strength=2.0): lowered eviction spike amplitude by ~40%, re-warm time shorter. But p50 slightly higher steady-state (~2-3%) because soft-anchors kept a few cold pages resident that otherwise would have been evicted.
- Hard-pin (pin 50 pages): eliminated eviction-related tail spikes, but baseline memory usage up ~2.1% and sustained bandwidth slightly higher due to background refreshes. On limited-GPU configs this caused earlier aggressive global eviction, hurting unrelated tenants in multitenant staging runs.

Notable anomalies and notes to self:
- When prefetch-window > 4, we saw read amplification that saturates memory BW; small prefetch window (1-2) was best tradeoff.
- Decay-based unpin (halving anchor score every 30s) handled slow hotset drift better than fixed TTL because it gracefully releases pages.
- Certain pages show extremely long KV lifetimes (>=12h) and are clearly application state rather than working context; these should be candidates for different residency class (sticky vs working).

Metrics / sample numbers (from dev run logs):
- Baseline eviction rate: 12 evictions/s; during shift window peak: 27 evictions/s.
- Soft-anchor eviction rate: baseline 9 evictions/s; peak 15 evictions/s.
- Memory BW baseline: 65 GB/s; peak during re-warm: 110 GB/s (dev VM numbers exaggerated vs prod).
- p99 latency baseline: 32ms; during shift: 41ms. Soft-anchor p99 during shift: 35ms.

Operational impact considerations:
- Hard-pinning is dangerous in multi-tenant Dedicated unless pinned set is tightly budgeted per-tenant; could lead to starvation.
- Soft-anchors + decay are promising as default: they reduce tail spikes and don't permanently consume capacity. Need to tune decay half-life by workload class.
- Add a telemetry tag for "anchored" pages in observability so we can track anchor churn across rollouts.

Suggested changes to runtime heuristics (short list):
- Introduce 3-tier residency class: sticky (manual long-lived), anchored (auto-detected via recency+frequency), working (LRU). Anchored pages get decay unpin and a small protected headroom.
- Limit prefetch window to <=4 by default; backoff if device BW > 80% or eviction rate rising.
- On hotset-shift detection (detect change in center-of-mass of hotset > threshold): temporarily reduce anchoring strength to avoid long-tailed retention of now-irrelevant pages.
- Expose "anchoring profile" per customer (safeguard: dedicated pools can opt-in to hard-pin for SLA-critical workloads).

Next steps / experiments to run on staging dedicated pool:
1) Run slow-drift test (shift every 10m) with decay half-life sweep [15s, 60s, 300s] and measure 99th percentile and memory BW.
2) Run fast-snap test (shift every 30s) with prefetch-window sweep [0,1,2,4] and anchor-strength sweep (1.0, 1.5, 2.0, inf).
3) Multi-tenant stress test: pin 50 pages per tenant across 4 tenants to see global starvation thresholds.
4) Instrument tracing: add anchor-score tags to per-token traces and record eviction cause (pressure vs free-slot).

Action items (owner / ETA):
- Asha: wire anchor-score into telemetry pipeline and add dashboard tiles (ETA 1w).
- Miguel: prepare staging job configs & synthetic trace generator improvements (ETA 2w).
- Noah: run multi-tenant stress tests and collect kernel-level page-fault metrics (ETA 2w).
- Lauren: synthesize runbook and final recommendation for ops playbook (ETA 3w).

Open questions / risks:
- How often do anchored pages correspond to user-session-specific persistent state (should be sticky) vs ephemeral working context? Need to cross-check with application-level traces.
- Are there pathological workloads that intentionally move small hotsets rapidly to cause denial-of-service via re-warm BW? Might need rate-limiting on prefetch.
- Interaction with quantized model variants: smaller quantized weights might change page sizes / access patterns and the heuristics could need re-tuning per model family.

Notes / stream-of-consciousness (scratch):
- Might be worth a lightweight ML classifier for anchored vs sticky vs working using features: hit-rate last 5m, inter-arrival variance, client-id cardinality, token-depth correlation. Cheap logistic regression could work and be interpretable.
- Consider a graceful global unpin API that ops can call pre-rollout to avoid re-warm after a model switch. Could be used during canary rollouts.

If this core idea seems useful, we should also coordinate with product (rollout console flag) and SRE (explainer for incident response). For now keep experiments isolated to staging-dedicated to avoid impacting hosted customers.

-- end of notes --
summary: Exploratory draft on anchored-page behavior in KV cache. Tests show soft-anchors with decay reduce eviction spikes and tail latency at small steady-state memory cost. Hard-pin prevents tail spikes but is risky in multi-tenant environments. Next: run decay half-life and prefetch-window experiments on staging and add telemetry for anchored pages.
